description: What each shipped saved search should return when the app is deployed against sample_events/. Generated numbers come from the same run_pipeline the determinism tests call; the expected-empty entries are stated with the reason, because a search returning nothing is the failure mode this whole app is careful about and it must be possible to tell a correct empty from a broken one.
corpus: tests/morpheus/determinism/estate_pipeline.py, session_pipeline.py, network_pipeline.py, transport_pipeline.py, presentation_pipeline.py, application_pipeline.py, saas_pipeline.py, endpoint_pipeline.py, host_score_pipeline.py, campaign_pipeline.py, context_pipeline.py and telemetry_pipeline.py, rendered through SiemWireStage by make_sample_events.py

R-D-L1-001 - Transceiver substitution.why: One port. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/2's serial changed at minute fifty, from XCVR-sw1-Gi1/0/2 to XCVR-sw1-Gi1/0/2-B, on a poll whose link_flaps is 0: oper_status read up on both polls and the device's ifLastChange never moved, so the device says the link was never down, which replacing an optic cannot avoid. The other optic replaced this hour, on hq:sw1:Gi1/0/6 at minute forty-five, is quiet: its serial changed just the same, but ifLastChange advanced between the two polls and TC1FlapStage counted the drop (link_flaps=2, link_flap_unpolled=true), which is what a swap looks like. The notable names both serials, the replaced one carried from the port's preceding poll.

R-P-L1-004 - Optical degradation forecas.why: One port, the one whose optic was failing. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/6's receive level slid 0.04 dB every poll from the start of the hour until the swap at minute forty-five; the line TC1ForecastStage fits through its readings falls about 58 dB a day, and from the twelfth poll on the stage projects it reaching the 10GBASE-LR floor of -14.4 dBm within hours. Thirty-four polls carry that projection, and the search's stats BY entity_key reduces them to one row carrying the shortest. Nothing else projects: the tapped port's three-decibel step reads not_degrading on the poll it lands, where the slope is still within the noise, and nonlinear on every poll after, where the readings no longer sit on a line; the steady ports' jitter never stands more than two and a half standard errors from flat against the bar of four; and the optic that replaces the failing one begins a history of its own, too short to fit for eleven polls and not degrading after.

R-D-L2-001 - MAC address count exceeded.why: The rule joins port_designations, which ships header-only. Until an inventory populates it the lookup returns nothing and the join yields nothing. 17 candidate rows carry macs_per_port_first_in_window=true, so a non-zero result after populating the lookup is the signal that the join works.

R-B-L2-002 - Port-to-MAC binding novelty.why: Six ports. Two are the same two R-D-L2-001 would name if its designation list were populated, found without it. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/3 carried one address in each of the six snapshots before the hub arrived at minute thirty; the snapshot that carried the hub's four addresses raised its count to five, four above the most the port had ever carried, and each of those four rows is new to the window and a step. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/2 carried one address for nine snapshots and then the spoofed address beside it at minute forty-five, one above its own record. The search's stats BY port_key reduces the five rows to one notable per port. Every later snapshot on both ports has a baseline that absorbed the step, so the rule fires once per step rather than once per snapshot; and the peer switch's ports, which the estate met inside this hour, have no baseline to step above. The other four are the campaign's headquarters desk ports, hq:hq-sw1:Gi1/0/41 to 44, each of which carried its desk's workstation alone through the afternoon's walks until the walk after an intrusion found a second address, one above the port's record: R-C-003's single-board computer, the laptop of the fleet's own vendor, the printer and the second single-board computer. The rule cannot tell the attacker from the three controls, which is what the chain is for.

R-D-L2-003 - ARP anomaly.why: The search aggregates BY arp_sender_ip, so the 24 contested observations collapse to one notable for the one address that is contested by two MACs.

R-D-L2-004 - MAC in two places at once.why: One address claimed on a peer switch inside a single poll sweep (conflict, zero gap) and one displaced two seconds later. Both are inside the 60-second threshold. The roaming device, displaced a whole poll cadence later, is deliberately outside it.

R-D-L2-005 - Authorization without authe.why: One authorization on a port whose own exchanges were long finished, and one that arrived while a legitimate exchange on its port was still open. The second only appears because exchanges are keyed by device; keyed by port it would have paired with the innocent device's request.

R-B-L3-001 - Fan-out expansion.why: One notable, for the scanner, and now against the host's own fortnight rather than a literal. 10.0.0.50 reached its three servers in every working hour of fourteen days and then 5, 20, 45 and 80 internal destinations in successive scored hours: every scored hour is a step above that history, and the last clears the floor of fifty the rule keeps from the literal it shipped with, so 30 flows contribute. The DHCP server is the control the step answers: its Monday-morning conflict checks reach sixty internal addresses, which the literal fired on every Monday, and its own Mondays reach sixty-four, so this one is no step. 10.0.0.60 reaches thirty addresses on the public internet every hour and fails the internal proportion. The scanner_allowlist lookup ships header-only, so nothing is excluded here.

R-B-L3-002 - Beaconing.why: One notable, for the pair 10.0.0.70:93.184.216.34, which exchanges a 512-byte message every five minutes for four hours. The negative control is 10.0.0.80, which makes plenty of flows to one file server at the ragged intervals a person produces and whose coefficient of variation is above 1.0 -- an order of magnitude above the 0.15 threshold. Grouped by flow_pair_key rather than by src_ip, because a host that beacons to one address and browses to five hundred others would have the beacon averaged away by a search keyed on the host. Five more pairs come from the campaign corpus, R-C-002's five hosts each sending a 512-byte message every sixty seconds; the rule reports all five on their regularity alone, and 40 more mature rows contribute.

R-D-L3-003 - Reserved-range egress.why: One flow, to 240.0.0.1. Low volume and high signal by nature, which is only true if the classification is right about everything else -- so what this number really asserts is that the other 410 flows are correctly classified as ordinary. The classification is parsers/ip.py's, through TC3ReachStage, so the search holds no copy of the reserved ranges.

R-B-L3-004 - TTL fingerprint shift.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.100, whose traffic starts arriving one hop short from the third hour onward: twelve flows, every one of them shifted by exactly -1, which is what a single interposed device costs. The control is 10.0.0.110, whose TTL never moves. The aggregate threshold of three shifted flows is what makes this a statement about a distribution rather than about a packet, which is what the guide's rule asks for; a single shifted flow is noise.

R-P-L3-005 - Fan-out trajectory.why: Forty-three rows, and the fortnight of ordinary history the layer 3 corpus gained is why there are more. Eighteen are the planted scanner's: four for the scan, whose fan-out climbs 5, 20, 35, 45, 78 and 80 through the summary's five-minute bins, and fourteen for its ordinary mornings, one each, because a workstation reaching its three servers at five-minute intervals reads one, two and three in three consecutive bins. Eleven are the DHCP server's: seven on the two Monday mornings in the fortnight and four this Monday, sixty-odd addresses pinged across twenty minutes. Two each are the seven campaign sources whose fan-out rises through three bins in a row. The rule reads shape and not level or history, so the ordinary first minutes of a host's day read as an expansion; that is recorded rather than tuned away here, and measuring the rise against the host's own baseline is the obvious next condition. It was empty on the first two search-head runs because the search read the value two rows back inside the streamstats that creates it; it takes two passes now. A watchlist rule, so forty-three is not forty-three pages.

R-B-L3-006 - Fan-in onto a workstation.why: One notable, for 10.0.2.15, a finance workstation the inventory records as one. Its fortnight held one visitor an hour, its owner's jump host; in the third scored hour fourteen internal sources reach it, and the five flows that take the count from ten to fourteen contribute. Two controls: the DNS server, reached by eighteen clients this morning and by twenty on its own Mondays, never steps; the application server steps to fifteen clients when a new service is pointed at it, and is a server. Flows from the campaign carry no baseline and no destination role, so they reach no row.

R-B-L3-007 - First-contact upload.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.120's first flow to AS64666: nine megabytes out and three kilobytes back, an asymmetry near 3,000 against a fortnight whose most lopsided hour was its nightly backup at 6. Novelty is per host and permanent, so the first flow is the only one. Each half also happens alone and is quiet: a first download from AS64667 is a first contact without the shape, and the backup provider sent five megabytes, more than ever, is the shape without the first contact.

R-D-L3-008 - Port sweep.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.130, which tries forty ports on one internal server and is answered on each: the sixteen flows from the twenty-fifth port on contribute. The conferencing client 10.0.0.140 reaches thirty ports on its media relay, which is outside the estate, and the horizontal scanner reaches eighty addresses on one port; neither is this rule's shape.

R-P-L3-009 - Host drift trajectory.why: Three host-days after deduplication, from 24 rows that carry the trajectory: the engineering workstation planted to drift, on the last three of its seven scored days. Its daily mean reconstruction error against its peer group's model climbs every scored day, from 0.7 on the first to 379 on the last, and the rule reports it from the fifth rising day rather than the fourth: the fourth is the first day that meets both conditions, four rising windows by more than 1.5 of the host's own day-to-day spread, and the last the drift stage does not yet call mature, because maturity is four prior days observed and the scored week's first day is the first observed. The rule has neither of R-P-L5-006's ceilings. The host scores are uncalibrated where the fortnight never varied a feature, so this host's daily mean runs into the hundreds and its acceleration into the tens, and either ceiling would read the trajectory as not one; and no rule reads a host's score level, so there is no composite rule to hand a loud day to. The nine other hosts rise for at most three days: the workstation planted to change once scores about 70 from that day and does not climb, and no ordinary host's daily mean reaches 1.6. Watchlist, never a page: each firing is written to host_watchlist, which R-B-L7-004 reads.

Connection evidence - layers 3, 4 and 6.why: One connection, the campaign attacker's breach from 10.20.1.5:45000 to the sync server, which the flow exporter, the packet sensor and the inspection point each recorded and each stamped with the same Community ID. The four other exfiltrators' breaches were seen by the flow exporter and the packet sensor only, and R-C-002's attacker's new TLS stack's connection by the inspection point and the flow exporter only; the report wants all three. A report rather than a detection: it writes nothing to the risk index.

Host evidence - one machine across layer.why: Nineteen machines seen at two layers or more under one host_key. Ten are the campaign's workstations, resolved at layers 3, 4 and 6 through the campaign DHCP server's daily leases and the EDR inventory; the five R-C-004's breaches and handshakes come from were seen at all three, and R-C-002's five beaconers at layers 3 and 6. The other seven are client addresses the network and transport corpora both carry: both corpora resolve their clients through leases and inventory built the same way, so the same address in the two is the same workstation, seen at layer 3 in one and layer 4 in the other. The last two are the transport corpus's stack hosts, whose packets and HTTP requests both resolve to them, at layers 4 and 7; the first of the three, ws-0-60, is one of the seven, so it is seen at layers 3, 4 and 7. The campaign's servers are on static addresses no lease names, so their flows carry no host_key and their processes, which do, are seen at layer 7 alone. A report rather than a detection: it writes nothing to the risk index.

Identity walk - sign-in to switch port.why: Twenty-five sign-ins walked to a switch port through the lookups, every one to the port the pipeline resolved. Fifteen are the estate's desk sign-ins, walked by the 802.1X identity the directory gave each principal through binding_l5_l2. Ten are the campaign's host logins from leased desk addresses, walked by address to a MAC through binding_l2_l3 and the MAC to a port through binding_l2: R-C-005's attacker at both ends of the journey, and the controls whose addresses a lease named at the time. The sign-in from an address no lease names, and the one an hour after its lease ended, are walked to nothing, as the pipeline resolved them to nothing. Run after the three refreshes, or every lookup is empty and so is this.

R-D-L4-002 - SYN without completion.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.50, which sends a SYN to each of 60 destination ports inside one 60-second bin and is answered by none of them. The negative control is the workstation beside it, which opens connections to the same kind of ports in the same way and is answered: its flows carry three ACKs each and a syn/all of 0.14. The sweeper is a second control and a more interesting one -- every one of its SYNs is unanswered and scores exactly like the scanner's per flow, but it touches one port across thirty hosts rather than sixty ports on one, so a vertical-scan rule is right not to fire on it. 110 flows in the corpus satisfy the per-flow half of the predicate and one source satisfies the breadth.

R-D-L4-003 - RST ratio.why: Two notables from one predicate, which is the whole of this rule. 50 flows in the corpus carry refusals and nothing else, and they sit at the same rst/all of 0.5; what separates them is which side of the refusal fans out. 10.0.1.50 refuses 20 clients, which is a service outage and scores 10. 10.0.0.70 is refused by 30 servers, which is closed-port enumeration and scores 40. A rule reading only the ratio would return these as one kind of thing and send the wrong response to one of them.

R-B-L4-004 - Stack fingerprint mismatch.why: One notable, for ws-0-61: its HTTP requests claim Chrome on Windows, and in its second hour its SYNs carry the option order of a Linux stack, new to that host. A browser's User-Agent is whatever the software writes; the option order is whatever the kernel writes, and a Windows workstation emitting Linux SYNs is running a second stack -- a virtual machine, a tunnel endpoint or a tool with its own. The joins are on host_key, which is the one entity the two layers share, and not on a flow: the stack is read off the SYN at layer 4 and the claim off the request at layer 7, and a request rides a flow whose SYN may have been seen in another hour. ws-0-60 is the control: the same Chrome on Windows, over a Windows stack throughout. 10.0.0.62 runs curl over Linux and claims no operating system at all, so there is nothing for its stack to contradict.

R-B-L4-005 - Transfer envelope breach.why: One notable, for the triple 10.0.0.80:10.0.1.30:445, which transfers 60000 bytes against an envelope of 1200 -- fifty times its own 99th percentile. The negative control is 10.0.0.90:10.0.1.40:443, which moves more data in total and varies by a factor of two doing it: a global threshold would have to sit above the busy triple and would then sit above the exfiltration too. The envelope is a percentile rather than a maximum because the triple has 120 prior transfers, above the hundred a 99th percentile by nearest rank needs to be one; below that figure it would be the largest transfer ever seen wearing a percentile's name. Five more come from the campaign corpus: each of R-C-004's five actors' hosts uploads 1200 bytes to a sync server a hundred and ten times and then 60000 once, fifty times its envelope. The breach is identical in all five; whether the host belonged to the principal who had just exported, while their session held it, is what R-C-004 adds.

R-B-L6-001 - New TLS client fingerprint.why: Seven hosts from 13 rows. One notable, for 10.0.0.20, which presented one TLS stack across 34 handshakes and then a second. Two negative controls. 10.0.0.21's second stack is equally novel the first time it appears -- it had made two handshakes at that point, so the settled-history floor of twenty separates them; that control is the one the corpus had to be rebuilt to show. 10.0.0.23, a personal device, has as settled a history and as new a stack as 10.0.0.20, and no asset inventory knows it, so the managed-endpoint gate holds it back. Two more hosts are the week R-P-L6-006 reads: 10.0.0.24, planted to acquire a stack a day, is a settled, managed host each of the six times it does, with 25 to 150 handshakes behind it, and is six of the rows; 10.0.0.25 acquires two stacks and stops, two rows. The rule says each stack is new to its host, which is true of all eight, and nothing about whether the host keeps acquiring them, which is R-P-L6-006's to say. Four more come from the campaign corpus: R-C-002's attacker and three of its controls are settled hosts the campaign's inventory manages, twenty-four handshakes each, presenting a new stack once. The fifth control has five handshakes behind it and is held back by the floor. Which of the four went on to beacon to the destination it presented the new stack to, within the hour, is R-C-002's to say.

R-D-L6-002 - Certificate issuer anomaly.why: Three notables, grouped on the TLS destination -- the address and the server name together where the handshake carries one. 93.184.216.34 presented a proxy's authority for portal.example.com after a corpus of one corporate authority, which is interception. 93.184.216.36 migrated authorities legitimately, and the rule reports that once: the single-issuer gate closes on the next handshake, because the destination has now demonstrably presented two. 93.184.216.38 is a shared host fronting shop.example-hosting.net under a public authority and a mail service under a hosting provider's, alternating; the proxy's authority then appears for the shop. Keyed on the address alone, that host has presented two authorities from the start, the single-issuer gate never opens on it, and the interception goes unseen -- which is why the reference is kept per name. The control is 93.184.216.35, a delivery host rotating among four authorities, which differs from its own mode on 19 handshakes and is removed entirely by the same gate.

key_values.presented_issuer: CN=Public Trust CA G3, O=Trust Services, C=US
key_values.established_issuer: CN=Public Trust CA G2, O=Trust Services, C=US
CN=Public Trust CA G2, O=Trust Services, C=US

R-D-L6-003 - Self-signed to external des.why: One notable, for 93.184.216.37, over two connections carrying a self-signed certificate valid for three days. Eight handshakes in the corpus carry a self-signed certificate and six of them are the internal appliance at 10.0.1.50 -- a management interface nobody bought a certificate for, which is what an estate has hundreds of. The classification is parsers/ip.py's, through the same module TC3ReachStage uses, so the search holds no copy of the reserved ranges.

R-B-L6-004 - Cipher downgrade.why: One notable, for the pair 10.0.0.22:93.184.216.34, which negotiated modern suites ten times and then a broken one. Two controls: the varied host's conversations move between two sound suites routinely, which a reference taken as a mode rather than a minimum would have called a downgrade every time the weaker one was chosen, and the legacy appliance pair sits at a low floor permanently without ever falling below it.

R-D-L6-005 - Content type mismatch.why: One notable: an archive behind a declared PNG. 50 handshakes in the corpus carry both content types and reach the comparison, and 49 of them are re-encodings -- a declared PNG detected as a JPEG, which is a thumbnailer or a client guessing from the extension. A rule comparing types rather than categories would return all 50.

R-P-L6-006 - Client stack trajectory.why: Three host-days after deduplication, from 72 rows that carry the trajectory: 10.0.0.24, the workstation planted to acquire a TLS stack a day, on the last three of its seven days. It makes 24 handshakes to the vendor's update host every day, so each day's hourly rows carry the day's distinct-stack count under the daily seal, and that count climbs one a day from one to seven. The rule reports it from the fifth day rather than the fourth, as R-P-L3-009 does: the fourth is the first day that meets both conditions, four rising windows by more than 1.5 of the host's own day-to-day spread, and the last the drift stage does not call mature, because maturity is four prior days observed and the week's first day is the first observed, so its 24 rows meet the conditions with drift_mature=false and are not counted. R-B-L6-001 fires on each of the six acquisitions too, because each new stack appears to a settled, managed host: the two rules read the same handshakes and say different things, one that a stack is new to the host, the other that the host keeps acquiring them. The control, 10.0.0.25, acquires a second stack on its second day and a third on its third and then holds at three: its rise is three windows, one short, and when the count stops rising the rising count returns to one, so it never watchlists. Every other client, the campaign's included, either makes all its handshakes in one day or presents the same stack day after day, so none rises past one. Watchlist, never a page: every firing is written to host_watchlist, keyed on the host the lease names, ws-0-24, the rule and the day.

TLS table coverage - unrecognized values.why: One summary row, and the value is in the numbers rather than in whether it fired. Both zero here, which is what makes the five counts above mean what they claim: a corpus that had drifted outside the cipher ordering or the media type map would make those rules fire less and say nothing about why. In a real estate this is the search that reveals an inspection point emitting OpenSSL short names rather than IANA ones, which lands the entire cipher feed in unrecognized_ciphers.

R-B-L7-001 - DNS tunneling.why: One notable, for evil-tunnel.com in its event hour: 129 distinct subdomains, every one random and long-labelled, from one client whose busiest day before it held one. The 130th query is the hour's first, when the client had asked for one subdomain and stood at once its busiest day, so the baseline condition holds it back. Each condition has a control that it alone keeps quiet. cdn-assets.net clears entropy and the count and fails only on label length -- the guide's own warning that entropy alone flags every content delivery network. tenant-saas.com clears entropy and length on all 30 of its queries and fails only on the count, because it is one hostname asked for repeatedly. saas-provider.com has 130 ordinary subdomains and fails both per-query conditions. filerep-av.net is a reputation agent looking up file hashes as random, long subdomains: 100 an hour every day for a week, which is the floor and not above it, and 120 on the event day, which clears the floor and is 1.2 times its busiest day -- the baseline condition alone keeps it quiet, and the 820 rows it puts through the per-query conditions are most of the 1228. Its first week is held to the literal alone, because a client with fewer than seven days of history has no baseline to be measured against. slow-tunnel.net is R-P-L7-009's client: 248 queries over eight days that clear entropy and length on every one, ten subdomains on the first day and six more each day after, so its 52 on the event day are half the floor and 1.13 times its busiest day, and the count condition keeps it quiet on every day -- a tunnel paced under the literal, which is what the trajectory rule beside this one reads. The count is taken per domain and hour over qualifying queries in the search rather than read off the row, so all four conditions hold for the same traffic.

R-D-L7-005 - Enumeration.why: Two notables. 10.0.0.40 requested 220 distinct paths and was refused on nine in ten, with curl, after a week of requesting a few paths a day as Chrome -- 22 times its busiest day. 10.0.0.41 requested as many and was refused on every one, so its 4xx:2xx ratio is undefined on every row -- it appears only because the search tests 4xx > 0.7 * 2xx rather than thresholding the ratio column, and a search written the other way would lose the client the rule is most for. It has no history, so the literal alone holds it. The crawler requests as many distinct paths and is refused on one in twenty; the broken client is refused on every request but asks for one path. 10.0.0.45 is an authorized scanner that requests 200 paths a day and is refused on most: on the event day it requests 220, clearing the literal and the refusal condition, and is 1.1 times its busiest day, so the baseline condition alone keeps its 20 rows out. Each control fails exactly one condition.

R-B-L7-007 - Service reached by new clie.why: One notable, for payroll-api.corp.example:443 in the event hour: three application servers reach it every day, and in that hour fifteen clients do -- five times its busiest day -- one of them presenting a client fingerprint the service has never seen. It sits behind the reverse proxy at 10.0.2.10:443, so the service key is its name and the application context is the proxy's: corp-edge-proxy, owned by platform. Each control fails one condition. wiki.corp.example shares that address and port and grows from ten readers to twenty-five, 2.5 times its busiest day, all on the browsers it always sees; keyed on the address, the two names would be one service and the wiki's growth would read as the payroll's. 10.0.2.20:8443 carries no name, so it is keyed on its address: twelve agents a day and twelve on the event day, one of them upgraded to a new fingerprint. ci.corp.example goes from two clients to five with a new tool, which is 2.5 times its busiest day but fewer than ten clients. newapp.corp.example is reached by fifteen clients on its first day, and with no week of history it has no baseline -- the rule requires one, because a service's first day is its own change.

R-B-L7-008 - Domain generation.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.36: 80 registered domains in an hour, nine in ten of them answered NXDOMAIN, after a week of six a day -- 13.3 times its busiest day. A domain generation algorithm walks a list of names of which only the few its operator registered resolve, so many distinct domains and mostly non-existent answers together are its shape. The controls fail one condition each. 10.0.0.38 is a busy browser reaching 70 domains, every one of which resolves. 10.0.0.39 is a link checker that tries 50 domains a day and finds most dead: on the event day it tries 60 with 78 percent NXDOMAIN, clearing both literals, and is 1.2 times its busiest day, so the baseline condition alone keeps it quiet. The NXDOMAIN share is read only once a client has asked twenty questions in the window, so a client whose first two lookups fail is not a 100 percent failure rate.

R-D-L5-003 - Impossible travel.why: One principal is authenticated from New York half an hour after her own office login in London, and then back in London ninety minutes later. Two rows rather than one is what a single interloper produces: the jump away and the victim's next authentication from where she actually is. The traveller who makes the same crossing in eight hours is inside the threshold and does not appear, and the VPN user whose apparent location changes country twice a day is excluded by egress range rather than alerted on.

R-D-L5-004 - Multi-factor fatigue.why: Five denials at ninety-second intervals and then an approval: six challenges inside eight minutes, which clears both thresholds. The fumbled password beside it -- two failed authentications and a success, with the factor never challenged -- is failure-then-success with none of the denial volume the rule requires, and does not appear.

R-D-L5-007 - Off-hours authentication.why: Four successful sign-ins at an hour the principal's own mature histogram had never held. alice@example.com at 03:00 is the planted case, an office worker who has only ever signed in during office hours. bob@example.com at 08:00 is real too: the sign-in from London before his flight to New York, at an hour his office week never used. That is what the rule is for, and why it is a notable rather than a page. erin@example.com fires twice, at 15:00 and 17:00 on the afternoon her account is used from Amsterdam: two of its hours her office weeks never held, and the first sign-in at each. svc-batch@example.com signs in at 03:00 every night and does not appear: the same hour is ordinary in its own history, which is the negative control that makes the feature a statement about a principal rather than about a clock. carol@example.com's 02:00 burst is at an unseen hour as well, and is left to R-D-L5-004 and R-D-L5-009 because its rows at that hour are refusals until the last.

R-D-L5-008 - New authentication location.why: Two first sign-ins from a new place by principals whose history is mature. alice@example.com in New York is the impossible-travel row R-D-L5-003 also reports, from the other side: there the speed, here the place. bob@example.com in New York is his arrival after the flight, reported once and never again, because the set the stage keeps is cumulative. dave@example.com's first sign-in through the Frankfurt concentrator is also a new place, on the first day of the training fortnight with one prior sign-in in his history, and the cadence_mature gate keeps it out: in a principal's first days every place is new because nothing is old yet. erin@example.com is the one this search misses. Her account's first sign-in from Amsterdam, on a device it had never used, failed, and that failed row is the one carrying location_first_seen and device_first_seen; every success after it is the second sighting, and the search reads successes only. An attacker who gets the password wrong once first is invisible to it. R-B-L5-001 and R-B-L5-002 find the afternoon; the gap is recorded in the retrospective rather than tuned out of the corpus.

R-D-L5-009 - Failed authentication run e.why: One run long enough to be guessing: carol@example.com's five refused attempts and then the approval. R-D-L5-004 reports the same burst from the factor's side, and two rules reading two columns of one event is correct rather than redundant. alice@example.com's fumbled password -- two failures and a success -- is failure-then-success below failure_threshold of 3, which is what most of an estate does on a Monday, and does not appear.

R-B-L5-001 - Composite authentication an.why: Forty-two rows, every one from a principal's own model, committed under examples/layer5_model/models/ and trained on the corpus's fortnight before the scored week. erin@example.com is the case the models exist for: twelve sign-ins one afternoon from Amsterdam, on a device and to applications her account never used, without the second factor -- nothing the deterministic rules call impossible -- and then eight more on Thursday and Friday from London, because the *increment features are cumulative and stay raised until a model is trained on a window that includes the afternoon. The other three are the week's planted departures: alice@example.com from her first failed password on Wednesday through Thursday and again in New York, bob@example.com from his sign-in before his flight, carol@example.com's six-attempt burst. dave@example.com and svc-batch@example.com have models and a week that repeats their fortnight, and do not appear; grace@example.com joins in the scored week, has no model, is scored against the population fallback, and the gate keeps her out -- with the gate removed her population scores cross neither threshold either, so the count without it is the same 42. The scores themselves are not calibrated: a feature the fortnight never varied has a training loss spread of a rounding residue, so any change scores in the thousands, and the thresholds of 6 and 2 read as 'departed from the fortnight' and nothing finer.

R-B-L5-002 - Location novelty anomaly.why: Twenty-eight rows from the three principals who reached somewhere new in the scored week: erin@example.com in Amsterdam and every row of hers after it, bob@example.com in New York, alice@example.com in New York and her next sign-in. The search reads the reconstruction error on locincrement, which is that feature's error given all ten rather than a flag for a new place: bob@example.com's sign-in from London before his flight fires because the hour is one his fortnight never used. R-D-L5-008 asks the deterministic form of the question and misses erin@example.com, whose first sign-in from Amsterdam failed and carried the first-seen flags the successes after it do not; this search finds her. Nobody without a new place appears, and the joiner's fallback-scored rows would not cross the threshold without the gate either.

R-B-L5-005 - Session duration anomaly.why: One session longer than its principal's own: carol@example.com's last working day ran eleven hours against four of eight, a ratio of 1.375 to her baseline, at the default severity because the identity context gives her a standard privilege level. alice@example.com and bob@example.com work their usual eight hours and measure at exactly 1.0, which is not beyond the baseline. svc-batch@example.com's last night is the longest it has had, at 1.25 against its baseline of four hours, and is excluded because the context marks it a service account: its sessions alternate between a ten-minute check and a four-hour run, and a percentile of two shapes says nothing. Without that exclusion it would fire, which is what makes the exclusion a condition rather than a decoration. The campaign corpus's sessions never reach the sample floor of four, so none is measured.

R-C-002 - TLS anomaly precedes beaconing.why: One chain, and the first time this rule has returned a row: it used to read the two detections' notables, which only exist once those detections have run, and now reads the scored events. 10.20.2.5, settled on one TLS stack across twenty-four handshakes, presented a new one to 203.0.113.100, and fourteen minutes later its beacon to that address matured. Four others do both halves with one condition broken and are quiet: 10.20.2.6 was already beaconing an hour before its new stack; 10.20.2.7's beacon went to a different address than its new stack; 10.20.2.8's beacon matured sixty-seven minutes later; 10.20.2.9 had five handshakes behind it, so its new stack is only new because the host is. Every one of the five beacons is an R-B-L3-002 notable, and four of the five new stacks are R-B-L6-001 notables, on their own. The new stack's connection is the one the beacon's first flow record closes, so the two share a Community ID and the pair comes from the flow record: join_method is hard:community_id. No control's fingerprint shares a connection with a flow, and each would be joined on its addresses.

Behavior summary - per-layer scores.why: One summary row per (five-minute bin, osi_layer, entity_key, lineage_id) over the 17796 scored events on `morpheus:score:l1` through `l7` and `morpheus:score:host`. It was 320 before the estate pipeline rendered these events: the same layers 1 and 2, plus the desk authentications made in that hour, which add their own groups. `peak_z` is null on every row but layer 5's scored week and the host segment's, because only TC5ScoreStage produces `max_abs_z`, and it leaves each corpus's training fortnight unscored; a null aggregate does not drop a row, so the count is a statement about the grouping, not about scoring coverage. The figures grew twice more as layers landed: layer 3 contributes 411 scored flows keyed on source addresses, layer 4 contributes 432 scored packets keyed on flows, layer 6 contributes 105 scored handshakes keyed on hosts, and layer 7 contributes 1180 DNS queries and HTTP requests keyed on the clients that made them, 1333 SaaS operations keyed on the principals who performed them and 1138 process starts keyed on the hosts that ran them, none of which shares an entity with the estate's ports and principals or with each other. The campaign corpus the chained rules are asserted on adds 308 flows, 82 host logins, 108 session records, 555 packets, 165 handshakes, 241 process starts and 555 SaaS operations on the layer 3 to 7 sourcetypes, sharing entities with one another and with no other corpus. The layer 1 figure grew by 61 rows and 13 groups when a sixth port joined the estate: the one whose optic is swapped with the link dropping, which is R-D-L1-001's control. The layer 5 figure grew by 280 events when the session corpus gained the fortnight its models are trained on, with two more principals -- the one whose account is taken over and the joiner -- so its rows reach the search head with null scores and no model version, as they leave the pipeline. The figures grew again when step 9 gave layer 3 a fortnight of ordinary history before its scored hours: the network corpus now contributes 1184 flows where it contributed 411, and the presentation corpus 130 handshakes with a personal device among them; the campaign gained a principal who reaches a workstation and the flows of its exfiltrators' breach connections. And again when step 10 gave the port, the link, the VLAN and the 802.1X exchange behaviour of their own: the layer 1 stream grew from 305 polls of five ports to 793 of thirteen, the MAC table by 45 rows with a camera VLAN, a printer and a guest, and the 802.1X stream by 122 events from two lab benches reauthenticating every two minutes, 655 events in all. And when step 11 gave the SaaS corpus a second tenant whose sync service exports twice a day, 212 operations, and gave the layer 3 corpus one late flow, which goes to morpheus:late, where neither a detection nor the summary reads it. And when step 13 gave the application corpus a week of per-client history before its event day, so each client's DNS and HTTP rows are measured against its own busiest day: DNS queries grew from 440 to 1984 and HTTP requests from 740 to 2515, and the service class adds 303 connections keyed on the services they reached. Layer 4 gained 24 packets from the hosts whose stacks R-B-L4-004 compares with their browsers' claims, and layer 6 17 handshakes from the address that fronts two names. And when step 15 gave the estate's switches and router a poll of their own and put the campaign's headquarters desk ports in front of the rules: the device class adds 305 polls keyed on the devices, the campaign 292 port polls and 1125 MAC table walks on layers 1 and 2, which it had not sent before, and 12 flows from its four intruders. And when step 8's host segment arrived with a sourcetype of its own: 1568 rows, one per workstation per hour over three weeks, each its own group because the frame's event time is the hour's start and the entity is the machine, 536 of them scored and carrying a `peak_z`, which no row of any other layer but 5 does. And when the daily drift reached the TLS and DNS columns: the presentation corpus gained a week of 336 handshakes from the two hosts R-P-L6-006 is asserted on, and the application corpus 248 queries from the client paced under R-B-L7-001's floor, each keyed on the host or client that made it.

Chain assembly - cross-layer risk.why: Empty, and now for the plainest reason it has had: the risk is written and is not enough. Every detection ends by collecting its rows into `behavior_risk`, and this search sums those records per lineage, once each, over the chains the events span. 15 of the 3764 distinct `lineage_id` values span three layers -- a port's layer 1 samples, the layer 2 observations the ladder resolved onto it, and the layer 5 authentications of the person sitting at it -- and two detections accuse any of them, each a different one: R-D-L2-003, the address claimed by two MACs, at 55, and R-D-L1-002, the tap on the port Carol sits at, at 50, on the one window her desk sign-in shares with the tap. The threshold is `total_risk >= 60 OR (layer_span >= 4 AND peak_z >= 4.0)`, so 55 falls five short, 50 ten, and no span reaches four. The other 13 carry no risk at all; the search-head run records both totals. Every other risk record lands on a lineage of one or two layers, the 70 the layer 5 model rules now write included: a flow, a handshake, a query and a sign-in are each their own entity, and the chained rules, which do join entities, name each step's single-layer lineage. `methods` reads `resolution_methods`, every hop a resolver ladder took, and the `join_method` of every `morpheus:edge` record in the chain, which `EdgeEmitStage` writes one per hop and per connection carried between layers; the edges add no method the scored records did not already name, so the 15 say `soft:directory`, `soft:dot1x` and `soft:mac_table` between them where the single `resolution_method` named only the last, and 1455 chains in all carry one: the layer 3, 4 and 6 records now carry the two hops from address to machine, and each of those layers roots its chains on the machine where the hops reached one; the campaign's packets, handshakes and exports carry a third, to the session that held their address. That is also why there are fewer chains than the 4268 there were: a workstation's flows in an hour are one chain where each flow identifier, or each address a lease reassigned, used to be its own. A machine's chains are still one per layer, because each layer's corpus seals alone; the host evidence report joins them on `host_key`, and the host identity harness seals four layers together to show the chain they make.

Binding lookup - L2/L3 refresh.why: One row per desk address and five-minute bucket its lease covers: the campaign DHCP server's acknowledgements for the eleven desk addresses R-C-005's sign-ins come from and the four addresses R-C-003's intruders were given at headquarters, closed into leases by TC2BindingStage with each held for the term the server granted, and expanded with to_bucketed_records(key_name="ip", table_name="dhcp_lease"). Each row resolves the address to the workstation's MAC and to the switch and port the DHCP relay saw the request arrive on. The other bucketed rows are the MAC tables', the 802.1X supplicants' and the layer 1 history's, which this search's binding_table=dhcp_lease filter leaves out. The campaign's workstation leases, renewed daily for nine days, go to the same lookup in a deployment and are not rendered here: they carry no port, and at two and a half thousand buckets each they would outnumber every other sample event.

Binding lookup - L2 refresh.why: One row per MAC address and five-minute bucket a MAC table binding covers: the estate's 124, from the forwarding entries TC2BindingStage closed on the layer 1 and 2 switch, and the campaign's 1125, from the two sites' MAC tables the R-C-005 sign-ins resolve through, with the four headquarters desk ports R-C-003's intruders were plugged into. Each row names the port the MAC was behind; the refresh selects binding_table=mac_table and keys the lookup on the MAC the producer wrote as `key`.

Binding lookup - L5/L2 refresh.why: One row per 802.1X identity and five-minute bucket a supplicant binding covers: the estate authenticator's records, closed by TC2BindingStage keyed on the identity, for the three desk workstations, the two lab benches, the desk phone and workstation sharing one port, the MAC-authenticated device and the unknown supplicant. Each row names the port the identity was authorized on, which is the rung from a person to a port once the estate's directory has said which identity the person presents.

Binding lookup - L1 refresh.why: Twenty-three port intervals across thirteen ports: eight that never changed, two on each of the two ports whose optics are swapped partway through the corpus, two on each of the re-patched and the inserted-into ports, and three on each of the restarted switch's ports, whose neighbour was unknown for the first poll after it came back. Produced by TC1BindingStage from the TC-1 stream, which binds the optic and the LLDP neighbour port. The lookup is keyed on port_id and switch_id with no bucket, so a port's intervals collapse to one document and the row that survives is whichever the search wrote last -- which is why the search sorts ascending on bind_start before writing, making the surviving row the latest interval rather than the earliest. This lookup answers what is in a port now. What was in it on a given day is the history lookup below.

Binding lookup - L1 history refresh.why: Seven rows, one per port whose binding was ever superseded, and none for the six that never were. Gi1/0/2 and Gi1/0/6 had their optics replaced; Gi1/0/11 was re-patched and Gi1/0/12 had a device inserted in its path; and the restarted switch's three ports each split twice, the neighbour unknown for one poll and then back, which is two superseded intervals per port in the same day bucket. That last is a cost the history pays for a reboot, recorded rather than hidden: the binding stage cannot tell a neighbour not yet relearned from a cable pulled. A number close to the port count would mean the superseded filter had been dropped and the history collection had started carrying the whole estate once per day.

Binding lookup - L1 history expiry.why: The layer 1 history's maintenance search, on day buckets. It keeps every bucket inside the retention window and rewrites the lookup with them, so it returns what it kept, and every bucket here is inside it: the runner moves the events to the weeks before the run, and the refresh keys each row on the bucket its own time falls in. It was expected empty for as long as the refreshes keyed on the stored ordinal, a bucket counted from 1970 that an expiry measured against now() dropped; that zero was the epoch, not the job. The current-state binding_l1 collection has no expiry job: it holds one row per port, and a decommissioned port's row is the last true thing known about it.

Principal watchlist - expiry.why: A maintenance search that keeps only the watchlist entries whose expires has not passed. Its answer depends on how far the events sit behind the clock, and run_search_head.py places them: every timestamp moves by whole weeks so the newest event lands three to ten days before the run. R-P-L7-006 stamps each principal's entry with that principal's latest event, and both of its principals' latest events are three days behind the newest in the corpus, which is the host segment's last hour, so their thirty-day expiries are still ahead and the two entries survive. R-P-L5-006 stamps each principal-day it fired, and the latest of those days is more than thirty-five days behind the newest, so its six entries have passed and are dropped. Against the unshifted 1970 events every entry would expire, which is what this note said before the first search-head run showed otherwise. Run it last: run before R-B-L7-002, it empties the list that search reads.

Host watchlist - expiry.why: The hosts' list, trimmed as the principals' is. R-P-L3-009 stamps each host-day it fired with the day's latest row, and the drifting host's last three days are the newest events in the corpus, so once run_search_head.py has dated them they are three to ten days behind the run and all three entries are inside their thirty days. R-P-L6-006's three entries and R-P-L7-009's four are stamped with their hosts' latest rows in the presentation and application corpora's first week, more than fifty days behind the newest event, so all seven have passed and are dropped, as R-P-L5-006's are from the principals' list. Run it last: run before R-B-L7-004, it empties the list that search reads.

Binding lookup - L2/L3 expiry.why: The L2/L3 lookup's maintenance search. It keeps every bucket inside the retention window and rewrites the lookup with them, so it returns what it kept, and every bucket here is inside it: the runner moves the events to the weeks before the run, and the refresh keys each row on the bucket its own time falls in. It was expected empty for as long as the refreshes keyed on the stored ordinal, a bucket counted from 1970 that an expiry measured against now() dropped; that zero was the epoch, not the job.

Binding lookup - L2 expiry.why: The MAC rung's maintenance search. It keeps every bucket inside the retention window and rewrites the lookup with them, so it returns what it kept, and every bucket here is inside it: the runner moves the events to the weeks before the run, and the refresh keys each row on the bucket its own time falls in. It was expected empty for as long as the refreshes keyed on the stored ordinal, a bucket counted from 1970 that an expiry measured against now() dropped; that zero was the epoch, not the job.

Binding lookup - L5/L2 expiry.why: The 802.1X identity rung's maintenance search. It keeps every bucket inside the retention window and rewrites the lookup with them, so it returns what it kept, and every bucket here is inside it: the runner moves the events to the weeks before the run, and the refresh keys each row on the bucket its own time falls in. It was expected empty for as long as the refreshes keyed on the stored ordinal, a bucket counted from 1970 that an expiry measured against now() dropped; that zero was the epoch, not the job.

Binding health - unresolved rate.why: One row: the ARP stream, the one class whose records carry a resolution outcome. Its 180 unresolved of 1,220 is the corpus's planted rate (0.148), under the 0.2 that marks a class degraded. Four more classes -- the layer 1 port stream, the MAC table, 802.1X and the layer 5 host logins -- carry the resolution_method column with no value on any row; while the wire sent those as null, resolution_method=* matched them and the search reported four classes as resolving bindings with nothing unresolved, which is how this expectation read five until the first search-head run. An absent field does not match, so they are no longer counted as healthy when nothing about them was measured. The search used to read morpheus:score:l3 alone, a sourcetype whose producer never writes resolution_method; the retrospective's gap G24. An operational metric: the value is in the numbers rather than in whether rows came back.

R-P-L5-006 - Drift trajectory.why: Six principal-days after deduplication, from 15 rows that carry the trajectory. None of them is behaviour, and the search says so in its own comment. The two principals whose scored week repeats their training fortnight climb on its last three days: their daily mean_abs_z rises by hundredths a day, never as much as a twentieth, because the cadence features keep moving after training ends -- each ordinary sign-in makes its hour a little less surprising -- so each day sits a little further from anything their models were fitted on. The rule measures the rise in units of the principal's own day-to-day spread, and for a principal who never changes that spread is tiny, so hundredths read as several of it. The principals whose week does depart -- erin@example.com's takeover, alice@example.com's fumbled password and journey, bob@example.com's move, carol@example.com's burst -- all cross the mean ceiling of 2.0 and leave: those are R-B-L5-001's to report. The predicate is evaluated here exactly as the search states it, so a corpus change that adds or removes a firing shows up as a diff rather than as a search that quietly means something else. What a deployment should take from this: the drift path's first false positives are principals who do not change, under a model that does not move, read against a spread that is nearly zero, visible in `drift_baseline_sigma`. Every firing is also written to the principal_watchlist lookup, so after this search runs `| inputlookup principal_watchlist` holds six drift-trajectory entries for dave@example.com and svc-batch@example.com.

R-B-L7-002 - Bulk data access.why: Three notables, one per principal, and the classification sets each one's severity rather than deciding whether it fires. nate@example.com exported 5000 records from a restricted object against an export baseline of 54: 75. olga@example.com exported the same multiple from a public price list: 20. pat@example.com exported it from an object the inventory has never heard of: the default 40, with ctx_object_found=false. The controls each fail one condition: quin@example.com's 5000-record export is inside a baseline of 4978; sam@example.com's is 4.9 times theirs; rosa@example.com has twenty exports behind them and so no baseline; tom@example.com's export was denied and read nothing. nate@example.com also queries two to three thousand records all month, which is why the baseline is per operation -- pooled, the export would be under twice their normal. Five more come from the campaign corpus: each of R-C-004's five actors exports 5000 records against an export baseline of about 60, from an object no inventory in that corpus classifies, so each fires at the default 40. R-C-004 is what tells the one whose export was followed by a breach and a new issuer from the four that were not. The search also reads the principal_watchlist lookup and raises a watched principal's severity by 15, capped at 100. None of the eight is on the watchlist -- R-P-L5-006 watches dave@example.com and svc-batch@example.com and R-P-L7-006 watches ivy@example.com and kate@example.com -- so every severity here is the classification's alone. The weighting is asserted in test_saas_harness.py by putting a bulk exporter on the list.

R-P-L7-006 - Access breadth trajectory.why: Two principals watchlisted, evaluated over the whole corpus rather than the four-week dispatch window, which gives the same principals because every rise in it fits inside four weeks. ivy@example.com reached one more object type every week from week 3 to week 7 with the same group memberships throughout. kate@example.com did the same, and that principal's role did change in week 5 -- but the directory recorded it in week 9, so on every week of the rise the context attached to the operations said sales-users, and the rule could only know what was known. jack@example.com has the same rise with the same role change recorded on time, and is quiet because the memberships differ across the weeks. leo@example.com rises for two weeks only; mia@example.com reaches eight types every week and never rises. Both are written to the principal_watchlist lookup, one entry each, which R-B-L7-002 reads.

R-P-L7-009 - Subdomain count trajectory.why: Four client-days after deduplication, from 172 rows that carry the trajectory: 10.0.0.46, the client planted to tunnel slowly, on the last four of its eight days. It asks for random, long-labelled subdomains of slow-tunnel.net, ten on its first day and six more each day after, 52 on the event day, so each day's hourly rows carry the day's largest per-domain count under the daily seal, and that count climbs every day. The rule reports it from the fifth day rather than the fourth, as the other two trajectory rules do: the fourth is the first day that meets both conditions and the last the drift stage does not call mature, so its 28 rows are not counted. R-B-L7-001 never fires on this client. Its queries clear entropy and label length on every one of the 248, and 52 in a day is half the 100-subdomain floor; on the event day, the first with a mature baseline, it is 1.13 times its busiest day rather than twice. The literal reads a day, and this client never has a loud one; the two rules read the same column, dns_subdomains_per_domain, and a tunnel paced to stay under a literal is the traffic the trajectory rule exists for. evil-tunnel.com's client rises for two days, because its 129 subdomains come in one hour after a day of one; the reputation agent rises for two, 100 a day and then 120; no other client rises past one. Watchlist, never a page: every firing is written to host_watchlist, keyed on the host the lease names, ws-0-46, the rule and the day.

R-B-L7-004 - Process ancestry novelty.why: Four notables from the endpoint corpus, and the integrity level and the host's criticality together set each one's severity rather than deciding whether it fires. fin-01 started PowerShell from Word at high integrity, which nothing in the finance workstations' peer group had done in thirty days -- although the build servers do it every day, because another group is not a peer: 55 on a medium workstation. Its EDR has spelled it FIN-01 since day 20, and it is one host with one history throughout. fin-02 ran a remote-access tool at system integrity that it last ran thirty-eight days earlier: 70. kiosk-01, which the inventory knows, calls low and has placed in no peer group, started mshta.exe: judged on its own history, endpoint_host_only=true, 40 halved to 20. build-02's git started curl with no integrity level reported: the default 40, half again on a server the inventory calls high, 60. The controls each fail one condition: build-02 compiled with a pair it had never run and its peer runs daily; fin-03 started an editor installed under a different user's profile than the peer who runs it, and per-user folders are collapsed; kiosk-01 started Notepad, which it last ran on day 20; lab-01, four days old and not in the inventory, started nmap before any comparison was possible. Seven more come from the campaign corpus, on the hosts its eight actors reached: six servers the inventory calls high each started a process no host in the group had run, at system integrity, 105 apiece, and the finance workstation one actor reached did the same at medium, 70; the eighth started only what its server always runs. This rule cannot tell the one of them that followed a fan-out and a first login to a server from the others; R-C-001 is what does. Risk is summed per chain rather than read as a probability, so the weighting is not capped, and a system-integrity process on a high-criticality server writes more than any other single detection. The rule now reads the host_watchlist lookup R-P-L3-009 writes and raises a watched host by 15; none of these hosts is on it, because the host corpus's machines share nothing with the endpoint corpus's or the campaign's, so every severity stands as written.

R-C-001 - Lateral movement chain.why: One chain, and the first chained rule in this app to return a row, because it reads the scored events rather than other rules' notables. From 10.20.0.5, fan-out rose above its own previous hour -- to twenty-five new addresses, half what R-B-L3-001 fires on -- then dana@example.com logged in from that address to SRV-DB-02, a server they had never logged into, and seven minutes later srv-db-02, as its EDR spells it, started a process no server in its peer group had run in thirty days. The two spellings are one host because both pipelines render them with the same rule. Seven other actors each do all of that but one step, and are quiet: the new process ran before the login; the last step came thirty-five minutes after the first; the login was to the principal's own server; the login came from another address; the fan-out was a busy host's steady twenty; the server only ran what it always runs; and the host reached was a finance workstation, not a server. Six of those seven processes are R-B-L7-004 notables on their own.

R-C-004 - Staged exfiltration.why: One chain. kim@example.com exported 5000 records, eighty times their own baseline; twenty-five minutes later the address kim's session held open, 10.20.1.5, sent 60000 bytes to its sync server, fifty times that triple's envelope; and twenty minutes after that it connected to a destination presenting an issuer nobody in the estate had seen in thirty days. Four others each do all three with one relation broken, and are quiet: lee's breach and connection came from the address max's session held; nia's came twenty minutes after nia logged off; oto's connection presented the corporate issuer every host sees daily; pia's breach and connection happened before the export. Every one of the five exports is an R-B-L7-002 notable and every breach an R-B-L4-005 notable on its own. kim@example.com's sessions come from a domain controller that says logon and logoff, and the chain still fires because the search reads session_lifecycle, which TC5SessionStage normalizes to start and end. Each of the three steps carries the session_key of the session that held its address, resolved through the session intervals, so the chain is joined on kim's session rather than on the address: join_method is hard:session_key, and a deployment whose collectors carry no session key gets the same chain on the address.

R-C-005 - Credential replay across the s.why: One principal. quin@example.com signed in at headquarters from 10.30.1.11 and, twenty minutes later, from 10.30.2.21; the DHCP leases name the two workstations behind those addresses and the MAC bindings closed from the two sites' switches put them at hq:hq-sw1:Gi1/0/11 and edinburgh:edi-sw1:Gi2/0/21, 534 km apart, which is 1601 km/h. Five others fall one step short and are quiet: rhea's two ports are both at headquarters; sam reaches Edinburgh three hours later, at 178 km/h; tia's second address is not one any lease names, so no port can be claimed for it; uma's was leased to an Edinburgh desk until an hour before the sign-in; and vic's second attempt was refused. None of the six is a geolocation alert: every sign-in carries a resolved port or none.

R-C-003 - Physical compromise chain.why: One port and one device. At 16:05 on the campaign's last day the walk of hq:hq-sw1 finds a single-board computer, b8:27:eb:3c:00:41, behind hq:hq-sw1:Gi1/0/41, a vendor the port has never carried, on the same poll that saw the port's link drop for the swap; the DHCP server leases it 10.30.1.141, and thirteen minutes later that address opens SSH to the switches' management interface at 10.99.0.10. Three others each fall one step short and are quiet: a laptop of the fleet's own vendor on Gi1/0/42, no new vendor; a printer on Gi1/0/43, which only prints and never reaches the management network; and a second single-board computer on Gi1/0/44, behind the desk's own switch, whose port never sees its link move. The management VLAN is null on the row because vlan_designations ships header-only.

R-D-L1-002 - Optical tap step.why: One port. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/3 loses three decibels of receive light at minute forty while its transmit level holds, and every poll from then to the end of the hour reads at least a decibel under the median of the port's prior readings: twenty-one polls, which the search's stats BY entity_key reduces to one notable carrying the deepest deviation, -3.031 dB. The failing optic on hq:sw1:Gi1/0/6 slides a few hundredths of a decibel a poll and its median slides with it, so its deepest deviation is -0.867 and it is R-P-L1-004's; the two replaced optics change serial and are excluded on that poll, and no other port moves.

R-D-L1-003 - Link flap instability.why: One port. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/7 goes down and comes back in every polling gap from the half hour, which the device records in ifLastChange and TC1FlapStage counts as two transitions a poll; its hour's count reaches ten on the fifth flapping poll and every poll after it, twenty-seven in all, one notable. The single flap on hq:sw1:Gi1/0/1 is two transitions in the hour and the maintenance swap's, the re-patch's and the insertion's are two each; the restarted switch's transitions are labelled link_flap_device_reset and excluded.

Device restart.why: Four rows. hq's sw2 restarts at minute thirty: its own poll reads the uptime gone backwards, and the first poll after it reports counter_reset and link_flap_device_reset on each of the switch's three ports, so the device and its three ports are one row. sw5 is polled only as a device and restarts in a storm -- once in the period from minute thirty-five, twice in the one from forty, three times in the one from forty-five -- which is a row for each period, carrying how many restarts it held. An operational report: it writes nothing to the risk index.

R-B-L1-005 - Error rate step.why: One port. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/8's CRC errors climb by thirty more each minute than the last from minute forty-five, and every one of its sixteen polls from then stands more than 0.1 errors a second above the highest five-minute peak of the port's own history, which the climb itself joins period by period. Every other port runs a few errors a minute and never stands more than 0.0167 a second above its own record; the restarted ports carry no rate on the poll whose delta covers the uptime.

R-D-L1-006 - LLDP neighbor change.why: Two ports, one row each: hq:sw1:Gi1/0/11 re-patched at minute thirty-five from dist-sw3 to dist-sw4, and hq:sw1:Gi1/0/12, which at minute thirty-eight reports a neighbour the estate has never seen, 00:1b:21:7f:3a:01 -- a device inserted between the access switch and its distribution switch. Both changes took the link down, as cabling does. The restarted switch's three ports report no neighbour on their first poll back and their old one on the next: two changes each and no neighbour any of them has not had, so none fires.

R-B-L1-007 - Interface volume departure.why: Two ports, one each way, for the five polls from minute fifty until the next five-minute period's peak and trough join the history: hq:sw1:Gi1/0/9 sends nine hundred megabits a second where it never carried more than about sixty, and hq:sw1:Gi1/0/10, which never went quiet, carries nothing with its link up. Every other port carries what it always has, a tenth either way, and the restarted ports carry no rate on the poll after the restart.

R-D-L1-008 - Configuration change outsid.why: One device. hq's sw1 has its configuration pushed at minute two, inside the estate's change window of the hour's first ten minutes, and changed again at minute forty, outside it: the second is the row, and the configuration is one the device has never run. No other device's configuration changes, and the push inside the window is a change the rule must not read.

R-P-L1-009 - Reboot-rate trajectory.why: One poll. hq's sw5 restarts once in the period from minute thirty-five, twice in the one from forty and three times in the one from forty-five, so its third restart in the third period is the third period running with more restarts than the one before, on a baseline mature after six periods. sw2's single restart at minute thirty is a run of one, and is the Device restart report's.

Topology - LLDP adjacency.why: Fifteen links: one for each of the thirteen ports the estate polls, and one more on each of the two ports whose neighbour changed. The restarted switch's ports carry no link on the poll where they had no neighbour, rather than a link to nobody. The search merges with what the lookup already holds, so a second run writes the same fifteen rows.

R-B-L2-006 - New vendor on a VLAN.why: Three VLANs. hq:20, the camera VLAN, carried one vendor until a single-board computer appeared on it at minute forty, a vendor the segment had never carried; hq:10 carried one vendor until the hub's own MACs arrived at minute thirty, which is the hub R-B-L2-002 also names. The third camera, of the vendor the camera VLAN already carries, is a new device and not a new kind and does not step. The third is hq:30, the campaign headquarters' desk VLAN, which carried the fleet's laptops alone until the single-board computer at 16:05 and the printer at 16:25: two vendors new to the segment, two rows and one notable. The laptop of the fleet's vendor is not a new kind, and nor is the second single-board computer, whose vendor the first had already brought.

R-B-L2-007 - Slow 802.1X authorization.why: One exchange: the first lab bench's at minute forty-five took three attempts and succeeded nine seconds after the last, three times the slowest of the port's twenty-two prior exchanges, which is what its 99th percentile is below a hundred. The desk ports reauthenticate every fifteen minutes and never have the twenty prior exchanges a distribution needs inside the hour.

R-B-L2-008 - Instant 802.1X authorizatio.why: One exchange: the second lab bench's at 2940 seconds was accepted in the second it was requested, where each of the twenty-four before it took four. The two bypasses carry no elapsed time at all, which is R-D-L2-005's signal and not this rule's.

Pipeline health - refusal rate.why: One row: the DMZ poller, snmp-poller-dmz, whose three polls of sw3 arrive with clock_source ntp_undisciplined and a reported offset of 4500 ms, past EnvelopeValidateStage's one-second bound. All three were quarantined and none delivered, so its refusal rate is 1.0, and quarantine_reasons names clock_offset_exceeded. Every other collector in every corpus delivered everything it sent: no stage refused a clock, because no corpus row is more than a day ahead of its stream, and no envelope is invalid.

Collector health.why: One collector: arp-sensor, which numbered three ARP observations twenty minutes into the estate's hour and never delivered them, so its sequence skips three. No collector repeats or goes back on a number, every reported offset is within twenty milliseconds of true, and every record reached the pipeline two seconds after the sensor saw it, which is what the replay's ingest clock stamps. The DMZ poller's offset is not here because none of its records reached a window: its clock is the refusal rate's to report.

Late arrivals by class.why: One row: the layer 3 corpus's quiet host, one of whose flows from the second hour reached the collector in the last hour, after its window had sealed. WindowSealStage emitted it marked is_late and window_complete=false, and make_sample_events.py routed it to morpheus:late rather than to morpheus:score:l3, so no detection read it. Its flow is ordinary; what it tests is the route.

Platform baseline step.why: One step: the SaaS corpus's second tenant, labs, whose sync exported two records a run twice a day for seven weeks and four a run for its last two days. The first doubled run is twice the feed's thirty-day peak of two, and the next run holds there, so the step fires on the second; the run after that is measured against a peak of four and does not. The layer 5 corpus's identity provider reaches ten sign-ins in one hour against a peak of five and falls back to five the next, which is a burst and not a platform step, and every other collector, class and tenant in every corpus stays under twice its own peak.
